summaries.example: Imagine a tiny quantum experiment that can give a red result or a blue result. In the many-worlds interpretation, one world contains a person seeing red, while another contains a person seeing blue. Before the experiment, there is one shared past. Afterward, there are different future versions, each remembering the same past but seeing a different result.
summaries.summary: The many-worlds interpretation, or MWI, is an account of quantum mechanics in which the Universe has one quantum state, but our familiar world is only one of many world-like patterns within it. When a quantum event has different possible results, all of those results occur, each in a different branch or world. A person before the event has a unique remembered past, but afterward there are several versions, each connected to the same past and seeing a different result. MWI aims to explain why experiments seem to have one definite answer without adding a random collapse of the quantum state. It also aims to avoid action at a distance. The interpretation still faces questions about how to define a world, how to connect the quantum state to everyday experience, and how to understand probability when every result occurs.
key_ideas: The many-worlds interpretation says that many worlds exist within one Universe.
When a quantum experiment has several possible results, every result occurs in a different world.
Each version of a person remembers one definite past, but the future can contain many versions of that person.
The theory keeps the ordinary quantum equation and does not add a special collapse event.
The meaning of a world and the connection between mathematics and experience are partly approximate and debated.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantum mechanics works extremely well, but its mathematical description can seem to allow several results at once while our experience shows one result. The many-worlds interpretation offers one way to address this puzzle by treating all the results as real in different worlds. It also gives students a chance to connect physics with questions about identity, probability, explanation, and what counts as a complete scientific theory. It is an interpretation under continuing discussion, not an idea on which everyone agrees.

important_terms.definition: A proposed way to understand quantum mechanics in which all the possible results of a quantum event occur in different worlds.
The complete quantum description of a physical system, such as a particle, an object, or the whole Universe.
The one Universe that, according to this interpretation, contains many different worlds.
The process by which different possible results become separate, stable-looking worlds for observers.
The idea that a quantum event has only one result because the wave function suddenly changes.

questions_to_think_about: If every result happens somewhere, what does it mean to say that one result is likely?
Would two future versions of you be the same person, or different people?
Why might people prefer a theory with many worlds to a theory with one world and a special collapse?
Does a picture of many worlds explain what we experience, or only describe the mathematics?

summaries.example: Suppose a quantum experiment has outcomes A and B, with squared amplitudes giving measures of one-third for A and two-thirds for B. On the many-worlds interpretation, both outcome-worlds exist. Before learning the result, an observer can be uncertain about which successor-world she occupies, much as someone wakes in one of two rooms without knowing which room it is. The interpretation proposes that rational expectations should track the total measure of the relevant worlds, though philosophers disagree about whether this really solves the probability problem.
summaries.summary: The Many-Worlds Interpretation (MWI) treats the universal wave function as the complete mathematical state of one Universe, evolving continuously according to the Schrödinger equation or its relativistic generalization. It does not add a physical collapse when a measurement occurs. Instead, a measurement produces branches in which different macroscopic outcomes are recorded. A world is a classically describable macroscopic pattern—objects, people, and their states—used to connect the formalism with experience. The theory therefore has both a precise dynamical component and a less precise interpretive component. Decoherence helps explain why localized, stable macroscopic patterns are the relevant ones, addressing the preferred-basis problem for practical purposes. MWI also offers an unusual account of identity: an observer has a definite past but several future successors. Its hardest philosophical issue is probability. Since every outcome occurs, ordinary ignorance about which outcome will occur is not available in the usual way. Proposals based on self-location, world measures, decision theory, symmetry, or typicality attempt to recover the Born rule, but the source presents these as continuing debates. MWI is also discussed in relation to nonlocality, possible tests, Ockham’s razor, and rival interpretations such as collapse theories and Bohmian mechanics.
key_ideas: MWI has a mathematical part—the unitary evolution of one universal quantum state—and an interpretive part connecting that state with experience.
A world is not another universe. It is a macroscopic, classically describable pattern within the one Universe.
Branching gives an observer a definite result in each world, while preserving all the outcomes in the universal state.
Personal identity is unusual in MWI: an observer has one particular past but multiple future successors after branching.
Probability is difficult because all outcomes occur. Self-location uncertainty, decision theory, symmetry arguments, and other proposals attempt to recover the Born rule, but they remain disputed.
MWI is attractive to its proponents because it removes collapse and may avoid action at a distance, but objections concern its worlds, preferred basis, ontology, and probability.
summaries.why_it_matters: The interpretation illustrates how a single mathematical framework can support competing accounts of reality. MWI addresses the measurement problem by retaining unitary quantum evolution and treating definite outcomes as branch-relative rather than as results of a new collapse law. This may simplify the fundamental dynamics, while making the bridge to ordinary experience and probability more demanding. Studying the debate clarifies the difference between a theory’s equations, its ontology, and its rules for connecting equations to observers. It also shows why empirical success alone may not settle an interpretive dispute when rival views reproduce the same ordinary predictions.

important_terms.definition: An interpretation of quantum mechanics that treats the universal wave function as evolving without collapse and associates different macroscopic outcomes with different worlds.

The mathematical state that represents the physical condition of a quantum system; in MWI, the universal wave function evolves according to the Schrödinger equation or its relativistic generalization.
A macroscopic arrangement of objects in definite, classically describable states; in MWI, a world is a way of connecting the quantum state to experience rather than a separately defined universe.
The total physical system described by one universal wave function; MWI posits one Universe containing many worlds.
The apparent division of a quantum state into effectively separate macroscopic alternatives through interaction and decoherence.
The loss of practically observable interference between alternatives, helping stable, classical-looking structures emerge.
The question of why one decomposition of the universal quantum state corresponds to ordinary objects and experiences rather than infinitely many mathematically possible decompositions.
A proposed weight of a world, given by the squared magnitude of its amplitude; it is used in accounts of quantum probability.

questions_to_think_about: Can self-location uncertainty explain probability when the universal evolution is deterministic?
Is the squared amplitude a genuine probability, a measure of existence, or something else?
Does decoherence sufficiently explain why one basis of the quantum state represents ordinary objects?
Does eliminating collapse make MWI simpler, or does the large number of worlds make it less economical?
What kind of experiment could distinguish MWI from a collapse theory?

summaries.example: Picture a student who performs a quantum experiment while wearing a sleep mask. The experiment has two possible results, and afterward the student is placed in Room A or Room B according to the result. In the many-worlds picture, both result-worlds exist. When the student wakes but has not looked around, each version is unsure where she is. This is called self-location uncertainty. Supporters use an idea like this to explain why probability can still guide choices, even though every result happens in some world.
summaries.summary: The Many-Worlds Interpretation of quantum mechanics says that the Universe has one evolving quantum state, but that this state contains many worlds with different macroscopic histories and outcomes. A quantum measurement with several possible results does not cause the universal wave function to collapse to one result. Instead, each result is represented in a different branch, and observers in those branches experience one definite result. MWI therefore combines a mathematical claim about continuous quantum evolution with a philosophical account of how that evolution relates to experience. The idea of a world is not perfectly precise: it refers to familiar objects, such as people and measuring devices, in states that can be distinguished in ordinary practice. Decoherence helps explain why some arrangements—especially localized, stable macroscopic ones—act like the worlds we observe. MWI also changes how we think about identity. Before a measurement, an observer can be connected to several future successors, each remembering the same earlier life but recording a different result. This creates a challenge for probability. Several approaches try to explain probability through uncertainty about one’s location, the measures of branches, decision theory, or symmetry. The entry presents arguments for and against these approaches rather than treating the issue as settled.
key_ideas: MWI keeps the usual continuous quantum evolution and rejects a special collapse of the wave function.
A measurement does not select one universal outcome; instead, different outcomes appear in different worlds.
A world is a useful, partly approximate description of macroscopic objects in definite states, not a separate universe.
An observer’s past is linked to one history, while a quantum event can lead to several future versions with different records.
The probability problem is central: if all outcomes occur, supporters must explain why observers should expect outcomes in Born-rule proportions.
Supporters see MWI as avoiding some forms of action at a distance, while critics question its ontology, its account of experience, and whether it adds too many worlds.
summaries.why_it_matters: MWI is important because it targets one of quantum theory’s deepest interpretive puzzles: how definite experiences arise from a mathematical state that can contain several alternatives. It shows that changing one basic assumption—whether collapse is a real physical event—can affect ideas about probability, identity, locality, and scientific simplicity. The interpretation also demonstrates that a successful equation does not automatically tell us what exists or how observers fit into the theory. MWI remains a serious but disputed proposal, and understanding its disputes helps readers evaluate scientific explanations without confusing a theory’s usefulness with universal agreement.

important_terms.definition: A view of quantum mechanics saying that all possible measurement results occur in different branches or worlds within one Universe.
A mathematical description of the condition of a quantum system, including the whole Universe.
A large-scale arrangement of objects in definite states, such as a particular detector reading or the position of a person.
The single total physical system that contains the many worlds described by MWI.
The separation of different quantum alternatives into distinct, effectively independent macroscopic patterns.
Uncertainty about which world or branch an observer occupies, rather than uncertainty about which result exists.
The squared size of a branch’s amplitude, proposed as a weight for that branch.

questions_to_think_about: Is being uncertain about your location in a set of worlds enough to count as ordinary probability?
If the same person has several future versions, what should matter for decisions: personal identity or the welfare of all successors?
Why does decoherence make familiar, classical-looking worlds more stable than other mathematical decompositions?
Would removing collapse make a theory simpler even if it includes many unobservable worlds?
What evidence could separate MWI from an interpretation in which the wave function collapses?
